sections.content: How many people stayed in Newcastle upon Tyne after gaining qualifications?

Newcastle upon Tyne is a city in the North East. Newcastle upon Tyne also has a university.

Newcastle upon Tyne has higher levels of deprivation.

Overall, Newcastle upon Tyne ended up with:

  • more graduates than it produced
  • more non-graduates with advanced qualifications than it produced
Note: all towns and cities in this analysis are defined based on population size only. This means that some cities are classed as towns because of their population.

Let's explore this further

There were 10,225 state-school pupils from Newcastle upon Tyne who sat their GCSEs between the 2007 to 2008 and the 2010 to 2011 school years.

Of these, 2,800 (27%) went on to gain degree-level qualifications (level 6+ as defined by The Office of Qualifications and Examinations Regulation, or Ofqual ). We will call these people graduates.

Another 3,120 (31%) went on to gain other advanced post-16 qualifications, such as A-Levels, a foundation degree or higher apprenticeship (levels 3-5 as defined by Ofqual). In this tool, we will refer to these non-graduates with advanced qualifications as “qualified non-graduates", for brevity.

The charts below compare Newcastle upon Tyne to other English towns and cities using three measures:

  • what proportion of Newcastle upon Tyne's pupils became graduates or qualified non-graduates by the 2017 to 2018 academic year
  • of those graduates and qualified non-graduates, the percentages that lived in Newcastle upon Tyne in the 2018 to 2019 academic year
  • how many graduates and qualified non-graduates from elsewhere came to live there by 2018 to 2019, relative to the number who sat their GCSEs there

In some towns, some of this information may not be available because of small sample sizes.
The size and deprivation level of a town, as well as the qualification levels of older residents, were all related to students' educational attainment. Read our previous analysis.

Where did those who left Newcastle upon Tyne move to?

Of Newcastle upon Tyne's graduates, 715 were living elsewhere in 2018/19.

However, 225 of those graduates (31%) were living fairly locally, in the Newcastle travel to work area (TTWA).

Of Newcastle upon Tyne's qualified (level 3+) non-graduates, 595 were living elsewhere in 2018/19.

However, 365 of those qualified non-graduates (61%) were living fairly locally, in the Newcastle travel to work area (TTWA).

Of those in Newcastle upon Tyne's GCSE cohort:

  • 485 graduates left the North East
  • the most common region they moved to was London
  • 180 qualified (level 3+) non-graduates left the North East
  • the most common regions they moved to were London and Yorkshire and The Humber

In 2018 to 2019, 61% of graduates and 28% of qualified non-graduates living in Newcastle upon Tyne had moved there from elsewhere

In the 2018 to 2019 academic year, there were 5,220 graduates and 3,435 qualified (level 3+) non-graduates from our cohort living in Newcastle upon Tyne. This is compared with the 2,800 graduates and 3,120 qualified non-graduates who had lived there when they sat their GCSEs.

In 2018 to 2019, 39% of the graduates had also lived in Newcastle upon Tyne as GCSE pupils, while 61% had moved there from elsewhere.

Of the qualified non-graduates who lived in Newcastle upon Tyne in 2018 to 2019, 72% had lived there as GCSE pupils, while 28% had moved to the area from elsewhere.
